source: Davenport & Winet (2022) Pivotal voting: the opportunity to tip group decisions skews juries and other voting outcomes, PNAS
finding: Critique that the story model is thin on deliberation: real juries show a vote pattern that neither story coherence nor pure conformity predicts. In Louisiana (10 of 12 needed) juries pile up at exactly the conviction threshold.
numbers: Study 1, n=1,960 Louisiana jury trials: under 1% ended 9 to convict (one short, hung jury); 17% ended exactly 10 to convict; chi2=91.18, df=1, p<.001.
limits: Observational, so jury composition and evidence strength are confounds. Louisiana before 2018 only. Conviction side only.
agent_relevance: The final decision can reflect a wish to close the decision, not the best story. Do not read a final answer as proof that one story won. Log whether a stop rule, not evidence, ended the search.

source: Davenport & Winet (2022) Pivotal voting: the opportunity to tip group decisions skews juries and other voting outcomes, PNAS
finding: Experiments hold the other votes fixed and vary only whether the person can tip the group into a decision. Being pivotal raised voting to punish and raised belief that the target deserved it.
numbers: Study 2a n=261 preregistered: chi2=9.20, p=.002 (pivotal more punishing). Study 2b n=298 acquit side: chi2=0.03, p=.870 (no effect). Study 3 n=1,633: beta pivotal=0.46, SE=.12, p<.001 for vote; beta=0.49, SE=.20, p=.016 for deservingness. Study 4 n=505.
limits: Third-party punishment game with online adults, not real juries. Effect is asymmetric (punish, not acquit).
agent_relevance: Pressure to finish can rewrite private belief. If our scaffold forces a single answer by a deadline, expect belief to bend toward the answer that ends the loop. Keep a record of the belief before the stop rule applied.

source: Gill & Zungu (2023) What do other people think he deserves? Social influence on use of mitigating information, PLOS ONE
finding: Boundary condition: a narrative about an offender's life history lowers blame, but how much depends on what a fellow deliberator says. A confederate urging use of the narrative raised its effect. A confederate urging to ignore it had no effect on outrage or compassion.
numbers: Groups of 2 or 3 intro psychology students plus a scripted confederate; four conditions (deed only; narrative with neutral, ignore, or heavy-weight arguments). Pushing use of the narrative cut outrage and raised compassion; outrage mediated lower spiteful punitiveness. Ignore-argument: no impact.
limits: Students, small groups, a scripted confederate, written materials. Exact N per cell not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Narrative influence is moderated by one voice in the room. In a multi-agent scaffold, a single advocate for a story can shift weight on it; an advocate against it may not undo it. Give challengers a concrete alternative story, not just a call to ignore.

source: Cullen, Dilevski, Nitschke, Ribeiro, Brind & Woolley (2024) Impact of misinformation presented during jury deliberation, Front Psychol
finding: Deliberation can inject false details that jurors then remember as trial evidence. In Study 1, misinformation type did not change legal judgments, but pro-prosecution items were more often misattributed to the trial.
numbers: Study 1 N=275 (pro-prosecution, pro-defence, or contradictory misinformation in a deliberation transcript). Study 2 N=339.
limits: Participants read a deliberation transcript; they did not deliberate live. Sexual-assault vignette only.
agent_relevance: A shared story built in discussion gets contaminated by claims that were never in the evidence. Tag each claim with its source (evidence vs. another agent's statement) before it enters the case story.

source: Cullen, Dilevski, Nitschke, Ribeiro, Brind & Woolley (2024) Impact of misinformation presented during jury deliberation, Front Psychol
finding: Study 2: pro-defence misinformation was more often misattributed to the trial than pro-prosecution, rape myths moderated this, and exposure skewed judgments toward the defence. A judicial instruction about misinformation did nothing.
numbers: Study 2 N=339; instruction condition had no effect on memory or decision-making. Pre- and post-deliberation guilt ratings, recall and source memory measured.
limits: Direction of the bias flipped between Study 1 and Study 2, so the bias is not fixed in one direction. Moderated by prior attitudes.
agent_relevance: Warnings alone did not protect memory. Use structural source tags, not a reminder prompt.

source: Troop & Lagnado (2025) Case order effects in legal decision-making, Behav Sci
finding: Order of presentation changes legal judgments, which tests coherence or consistency theories. Moral-order effects replicate in civil and criminal cases and in individual and group decisions, but are asymmetric: one case stays stable, the other moves.
numbers: Five studies, total n=1,023, pairs of life-or-death legal cases, positive-first vs negative-first. Some later responses became less like the earlier case, not more.
quote: Responses to labile cases became less, rather than more, similar to responses to preceding cases.
limits: Vignette decisions, not full trials. Direction of the effect varied across studies (more similar in Study 1, less similar in Studies 2 and 3).
agent_relevance: Prior items change judgment of the next item, in either direction. Randomise or repeat order of cases and evidence in scoring runs; report order sensitivity.

source: Neal, O'Hara et al. (2025) Can jurors disregard inadmissible evidence? Multiphase Optimization Strategy, Behav Sci
finding: Failed replication of a classic: in Study 2 the inadmissible evidence itself did not raise conviction, and the standard judge instruction did nothing detectable. Only the four-part package lowered conviction, and only on a one-tailed test.
numbers: Study 2 n=624. Guilty: no inadmissible evidence 43.5% (70/161); instruction to disregard 46.5% (72/155); optimized package 37.2% (58/156); no objection 44.7% (68/152). Omnibus chi2(3)=3.14, p=.371. Direct effect of evidence OR=1.05, p=.823. Instruction vs package OR=1.47, one-tailed p=.049 (two-tailed .098).
limits: One hypothetical murder trial, online sample, effect depends on a one-tailed test. Study 1 was a 2^4 factorial that found a synergy among components.
agent_relevance: Even a famous effect (inadmissible evidence sways verdicts) can fail in a new sample. Our scoring should not assume a bias exists; measure it per task. Small interventions that stack (suspicion, reason, commitment, advice) may beat a single instruction.

source: Lages et al. (2024/25) Effect of verdict system on juror decisions: a quantitative meta-analysis, Psychiatry Psychol Law
finding: The answer format changes the result: adding a third verdict (not proven) cut convictions. This shows a story has to be mapped to a verdict category, and the model says little about that mapping.
numbers: 10 mock trials, 1,778 jurors. Convictions 28.7% (259/901) under three verdicts vs 39.2% (344/877) under two. Odds ratio 0.625, 95% CI [0.51, 0.77], p<.00001. Risk ratio 0.732; risk difference -10.5 points. Mixed-effects model: odds about 0.6.
limits: Between-participant mock trials from related Scottish studies; secondary analysis of published data, not preregistered.
agent_relevance: Output format is a lever worth 10 points of conviction. When scoring, fix the answer schema and test sensitivity to the number and wording of answer options.

source: Burd et al. (2025) Diverging decisions? A comparison of jury verdict procedures, Behav Sci
finding: Structuring the verdict with a special-verdict form (written questions) changed the outcome compared with a general verdict, with or without reason-giving. Applies to groups too.
numbers: Exp 1 N=267 (general, special, reasons-before, reasons-after); Exp 2 N=292 who deliberated as groups. General verdict jurors more likely to find for plaintiff than special-verdict jurors. Overall 66.2% found for plaintiff in Exp 1. Reasons before or after a general verdict did not change decisions.
limits: Civil defamation, one case. Two experiments, different formats.
agent_relevance: Decomposing a decision into sub-questions (like an element-by-element checklist) pushes toward the defence. A holistic story verdict and an element-wise verdict disagree; track both.

source: Authors from Univ. Nevada, Reno (2025) Words matter: attorney language abstraction and emotional valence, Behav Sci
finding: Surface wording of a case changes liability judgments, so story form is not the only driver. Concrete negative language raised liability; abstract language erased the difference.
numbers: N=273 after excluding 37; interaction F(1,269)=4.02, p=.046, eta2=.014. Concrete: negative M=72.2 vs positive M=53.0, d=0.65, p<.001. Abstract: 64.5 vs 59.0, d=0.20, p=.25. Manipulation check for abstraction failed (d=0.14, p=.26).
limits: Small interaction (p=.046), the abstraction check failed, written closings read alone, no deliberation.
agent_relevance: Concreteness, not just causal order, can move a verdict. Test whether our case summaries are concrete or abstract before comparing conditions.

source: St. George et al. (2026) Student- vs MTurk-generated samples: convenience, data quality, generalizability and outcomes, Behav Sci Law
finding: Conclusions depend on the sample: students and MTurk differed strongly on rape-myth acceptance and victim blame, and one effect (victim race) appeared only in MTurk.
numbers: Rape myth acceptance MTurk M=2.74 (SD 1.1) vs students 1.72 (SD 0.6), d=-1.04. Victim blame 2.99 vs 2.02, d=-0.92. Victim race effect on blame: MTurk F(3)=7.33, p<.001, eta2=.011; none in students. Victim gender eta2 .019 (students) and .006 (MTurk).
limits: Single vignette; effects small. Not a story-model test.
agent_relevance: A warning for any scoring on human-derived benchmarks: the human reference set changes what looks like a bias. Report which population labelled the data.

source: Xie (2026) Legal Evidence-Authority Dissociation (LEAD): reanalysis of memory contamination and AI advice, Front Psychol
finding: Reanalysis separates three stages: memory entry, judgment incorporation, and authority deference. Misinformation entered memory more clearly than it changed judgment, and mitigating facts moved sentencing more than the label 'judge' vs 'AI'.
numbers: Jury-misinformation data n=275; judge-vs-AI sentencing studies n=787 and n=860. Authority-source effect equivalent to zero within a preset small bound in Study 2; inconclusive in Study 3.
limits: Secondary analysis of three public datasets, individual mock jurors not completed juries, one Study 2 dataset not accessible.
agent_relevance: Remembering something is not the same as using it. Score memory use and judgment use separately; do not infer a story won from recall alone.

source: Pilot (Rutgers, 2026) The role of the dissenting voter on jury deliberation online, Behav Sci
finding: Direct data on the 11-1 to 12-0 flip: all six participants who started at not guilty changed to guilty after deliberation, against the hypothesized direction. Six virtual juries had a scripted dissenter.
numbers: 35 participants in seven six-person Zoom juries; 34 with verdict data; 6 of 6 initial not-guilty voters changed to guilty (significant paired shift). Collaborative conflict style linked to participation; predictor model did not improve fit.
limits: Pilot, tiny N, vignette, confederate dissent protocol, mechanism (evidence vs conformity) not separable.
agent_relevance: Minority views collapse under group discussion even when a dissenter is planted. A multi-agent review needs a protected dissent role, with a rule that a dissent can only be dropped when an evidence reason is stated.

source: Forensic Science International: Synergy (2022) Challenges to reasoning in forensic science decisions
finding: Review: automatic integration of information into a causal explanation is a strength and a risk. For causal reconstructions (fire scenes, pathology) the main failure is closing hypotheses too early.
numbers: Qualitative review; no pooled effect sizes extracted.
quote: In causal and process judgments, a main challenge is to keep multiple potential hypotheses open as the investigation continues.
limits: Narrative review, not a meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: Matches the story-model weakness: the best-fitting story crowds out rivals. Require at least two live hypotheses until a named test discriminates.

source: Systematic review (2024) The impact of rape myth education on jury decision-making, Trauma Violence Abuse
finding: Interventions for juror bias have mixed evidence: judicial directions, expert testimony and complainant statements sometimes change decisions.
numbers: 6,119 records, 3,202 screened, 8 studies met criteria (information vs no-information control). Findings mixed; internal and external validity limits frequent.
limits: Only 8 studies, mixed quality, no pooled effect.
agent_relevance: Small evidence base for debiasing instructions. Do not rely on a single debiasing prompt; measure it.

source: Perceived realism in juror decision making (2025/26, PsyArXiv preprint)
finding: Supports the narrative model with a twist: perceived realism, a feeling of a coherent story, was the strongest predictor of case-strength ratings and mediated the effect of recalled experience.
numbers: N=83 jury-eligible adults reading mock cases; variance partitioning and structural equation modelling; realism mediated explicit memory effects.
limits: Abstract only. Preprint, small N, correlational, self-report.
agent_relevance: A felt sense of realism can carry personal bias into the verdict. Coherence ratings should be calibrated against outside checks.

source: Singh et al. (2026) Suggestible judges: asymmetric conformity in LLM adjudication (Research Square preprint)
finding: Not a legal task, but it measures LLM-as-judge conformity to shown votes. A random label from a third annotator still moved verdicts for two of three vendor models; GPT-5.5 resisted.
numbers: 2,568 verdicts, 214 annotator disagreements, 4 conditions x 3 models. Random label C lifted verdicts by +6.5 pp (Claude Opus 4.7) and +9.3 pp (Gemini 3.5 Flash). FALSE-valued cues moved +10.5 / +16.7 pp; near zero for TRUE cues. Blind judge alignment with stricter annotator 68 to 74%, Fleiss kappa .68.
limits: Abstract only. SEC knowledge-graph pipeline, not courts; no ground truth, so manipulability not accuracy.
agent_relevance: LLM judges shown other voters may conform, asymmetrically. Run panels blind first, reveal votes later, and test a random-vote control.

source: Kalven & Zeisel (1966) The American Jury (recalled, not opened)
finding: Classic observation behind the 'thin on deliberation' critique: in most juries the verdict matches the majority at the first ballot.
numbers: Recalled figure: about 90 to 95% of juries with a first-ballot majority end in that direction. Not verified this session.
limits: From memory, number approximate; do not cite without checking.
agent_relevance: Deliberation mostly amplifies the initial majority; a model that explains individual verdicts may explain most juries.

source: Devine et al. (2001) Jury decision making: 45 years of empirical research on deliberating groups, Psychol Public Policy Law (recalled, not opened)
finding: Review states deliberation outcome is predicted by pre-deliberation distribution with a leniency shift and rare reversals; supports a narrow role for deliberation but leaves story form untested.
numbers: Recalled: first-ballot majority predicts verdict in roughly nine of ten juries. Not verified this session.
limits: From memory, not opened, number approximate.
agent_relevance: Treat as a to-do: open and verify before relying on the number.

source: Allen & Pardo; Heller (2006) rival accounts: relative plausibility and critique of narrative reasoning in circumstantial evidence (recalled, not opened)
finding: Rival accounts: legal scholars argue that proof is a comparison of competing explanations (relative plausibility), and that narrative reasoning can ignore base rates. These are theoretical critiques, not experiments.
numbers: No numbers; qualitative.
limits: From memory; page not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Use as the framing for a rival-story rule: always score the best explanation against the best alternative.

source: Search note (2026): no direct LLM test of the story model found this run
finding: Searches of Europe PMC and the search tool found no study that tests story-model predictions on language models. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, arXiv rate-limited; WebSearch budget exhausted.
numbers: None.
limits: Negative result from a limited search; earlier files (01) list LLM jury studies.
agent_relevance: The story-model-on-LLM test is open.

source: Davenport & Winet (2022) Pivotal voting: the opportunity to tip group decisions skews juries and other voting outcomes, PNAS
finding: Study 4: observers hold a voter more responsible when the voter blocks the group from a decision than when the voter tips it. This is a social cost for blocking, a likely reason for the cluster at the threshold.
numbers: n=505 vignette; beta hung jury=0.29, SE=.12, p=.021.
limits: Vignette judgments of third parties, not measures of the voters' own experience.
agent_relevance: Blocking an answer costs the blocker. In a panel, make 'no decision yet' a legitimate output so it is not penalised by the format.

source: Neal, O'Hara et al. (2025) Can jurors disregard inadmissible evidence? Multiphase Optimization Strategy, Behav Sci
finding: Study 1 of the same paper: a 2x2x2x2 factorial found that four cheap strategies (suspicion, a reason to disregard, a commitment, advising future jurors) worked together, not alone.
numbers: Study 1 was a 2^4 randomized factorial; a synergistic interaction led to the all-four package. Study 2 verdicts did not differ across groups at omnibus level (p=.371).
limits: Exact Study 1 n and effect sizes not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Layered, interacting prompts may work where one instruction fails. Test factorially, not one prompt at a time.

source: Gill & Zungu (2023) What do other people think he deserves? Social influence on use of mitigating information, PLOS ONE
finding: Mediation differs by social condition. With a neutral confederate the narrative worked through lower perceived control of self-formation, as in individual studies. With an advocate for the narrative the route changed.
numbers: Mediation on outrage and compassion; reduced outrage mediated lower spiteful punitiveness.
limits: Mediation from observational mediators in an experiment; small student groups.
agent_relevance: The same story can act through different reasons depending on the group. Record the reason a story was accepted, not only that it was.

source: Burd et al. (2025) Diverging decisions? A comparison of jury verdict procedures, Behav Sci
finding: Experiment 2 let mock jurors deliberate in groups, and the special-verdict form still shifted outcomes versus a general verdict. So the procedure effect is not an artifact of lone readers.
numbers: Exp 2 N=292 heard a mock trial, deliberated as groups; general verdict vs special verdict with reasoning requirement; plaintiff race (White or Latinx).
limits: Group-level analysis units and exact percentages not extracted.
agent_relevance: Verdict-procedure effects survive deliberation. Fix the decision procedure across arms when comparing scaffolds.
